newsitem.title: USA: Federal trial begins for Arizona governor.
newsitem.headline: Federal trial begins for Arizona governor.

text.p: Sixteen potential jurors were selected Tuesday on the first day of Arizona Gov. Fife Symington's federal trial on fraud, extortion and perjury charges.

Symington, a colorful, 51-year-old Republican, faces 22 felony charges. Federal prosecutors will try to prove to the jury that Symington committed fraud, extortion and perjury in connection with real estate deals during the last decade.
Seven prospective jurors were questioned in the morning session in U.S. District Court and all were placed in a final 39-person pool from which 12 jurors and five alternates will be selected.

In the afternoon, nine of 11 people were accepted into the final pool. Two were rejected -- one by the prosecution because she had problems understanding English and a second by the defense because she had signed a petition seeking Symington's recall.

When the 39 potential jurors are selected, they will face more detailed questions from both sides. The prosecution will be allowed up to nine challenges and the defense may ask for up to 13 to be rejected for specific reasons.
The governor's wife Anne and other family members were in Federal Judge Roger Strand's court as the trial got under way with no apparent extra security.
If convicted on even a single count, the two-term governor would be booted from the office he has held since 1991. He also faces a possible prison term.

Questioning of prospective jurors Tuesday focused on three areas: how panelists felt about bankruptcy and whether it would color their view of Symington; whether the rich and powerful should get a break from the justice system; and their views on labor unions, the apparent target of Symington's alleged extortion.

During the trial, expected to last 12 weeks, prosecutors will detail what they claim are lies told by Symington from the mid-1980s to the early 1990s, when he was a developer, to secure credit lines and business and personal loans.

The government contends Symington made false statements to lenders to prevent his real estate empire from crumbling. Prosecutors also will try to prove Symington extorted an agreement from six union pension funds to release him from a personal loan guarantee he made to obtain a $10 million loan for a shopping center in downtown Phoenix.
The government also will try to prove the governor lied under oath during court proceedings when he filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy in September 1995.
The charges stem from a probe into the 1989 collapse of Southwest Savings & Loan Association. Symington served on the thrift's board of directors.
After settling the case, the U.S. Attorney's office in Los Angeles continued its probe into the governor's financial dealings for several years. Last June, Symington was indicted.
Since then, there have been calls for his resignation by Arizona's largest newspapers, and his popularity in public opinion polls has slipped to 30 percent.
Symington, a descendent of industrialist Henry Clay Frick, has repeatedly maintained his innocence and has said he plans to seek re-election in 1998.
He has told the people of Arizona that he can continue to carry out the duties of governor while attending the trial four days a week.
